properties.occurrenceRemarks: Not certain what type of tree this was... but it was a good tree. Likely, a Sycamore, though by the time I began to take notice of it, it was in the final stages of decline. It reached up nearly 50 feet into the riverside skyline and at one time, with a full leafy canopy, must have been magnificent. Even dead, it provided a much needed bit of habitat in the midst of the concrete and constant traffic of the city. It first came to my attention as a daytime perch for a beautiful dark Merlin, spending the winter in Los Angeles. On my regular hikes through the neighborhood and along the river, it was one of the landmarks I looked for. I even learned to recognize, from hundreds of meters away, the dark spot in its upper branches that indicated the presence of a Merlin. It was also the home of a large group of Acorn Woodpeckers, who nested in a hole in its upper reaches and spent much of the day, when the Merlin was absent, patrolling its surfaces, searching for insects and storing acorns. I suppose that by loving nature and wildlife while living in a big city, I have become more sensitive to the needs of the creatures with which we coexist; so when I walked through the park on Friday and found one of my favorite wildlife locations gone, my heart sank. Of course, there are valid arguments for the removal of dead trees, but I think, to some, it was just an eyesore... and that is sad.
